summary: Updates RFC 8610 by addressing errata reports and making other small fixes to the ABNF grammar for the Concise Data Definition Language. CDDL expresses structures for protocol messages and data formats in CBOR or JSON.

plainLanguage.summary: There is a special language for describing the shape of data. People found small mistakes in its rule book, and this fixes them.

questions: what does rfc 9682 change in cddl
subtitle: Errata fixes and two small extensions to the grammar of CDDL, the language for describing CBOR and JSON data shapes.

tldr.problem: The ABNF grammar for CDDL in RFC 8610 had errata: string escaping was too permissive and lacked hex escapes, backslashes were lost in publication, and a few useful constructs could not be written.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the rules for string literals, comments and byte strings, lets a CDDL file contain no rules, and allows tag numbers and simple values to be given as types in angle brackets.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 8610 and its Appendix A replaces the collected ABNF in Appendix B of RFC 8610. Some changes are not forward compatible with tools that have not been updated.

today: RFC 9682 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2024. It updates RFC 8610, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Update Does
sections.content:
The Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), defined in RFC 8610 and RFC 9165, expresses the structure of protocol messages and data formats represented in CBOR or JSON. Its grammar is written in ABNF.

RFC 9682 updates RFC 8610 by addressing errata reports and making other small fixes to that grammar. The body explains the motivation for each change, and the updated collected ABNF in Appendix A replaces the collected ABNF in Appendix B of RFC 8610.
sections.plainLanguage: CDDL is a rule book for describing data shapes. This document patches the rule book where people found typos and gaps.

sections.title: Fixed String Literal Grammar
sections.content:
The old SESC rule for escapes in text strings was permissive. It allowed almost any character after a backslash, but it missed the JSON-style \uXXXX and \uHHHH\uLLLL forms that Section 3.1 of RFC 8610 implies (Erratum 6527). The new rule lists the allowed escapes explicitly and also adds a popular form, \u{hex}, where hex is the Unicode scalar value in hexadecimal. CDDL text strings do not use UTF-16 or surrogates, even though the surrogate-pair form is accepted for JSON compatibility.

With SESC tightened, the byte string rule BCHAR must now explicitly allow \'. Erratum 6278 pointed out that U+007F (DEL) was treated differently in SCHAR and BCHAR. The update excludes U+007F to U+009F, and the surrogate code points, from SCHAR, BCHAR and the comment rule PCHAR, using a new NONASCII rule. It does not try to exclude every non-printable character, to avoid tracking the evolving Unicode standard.

The same changes cover Erratum 6543 and Erratum 6526 (backslashes lost in the publication of Appendix G.2 of RFC 8610). The simpler approach for 6543 is to leave the processing of byte string content to a semantic step after the syntax is parsed. Appendix B of the RFC gives the details.

The new \u{hex} syntax is backward compatible but not forward compatible: files that use it may not work with implementations that have not been updated. The RFC recommends updating them.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule about special characters in text was either too loose or missing a way to write odd characters. Now there is one clear way, and some invisible troublemaker characters are banned.

sections.title: Escaping Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example defines six rules, a to c as text strings and x to z as byte strings. They show the string Domino's followed by a domino tile (U+1F073) and a place-of-interest sign (U+2318), written with \u{} escapes, with the JSON-like escapes, and unescaped.

All six come out with byte-wise identical content, 19 bytes each, differing only in whether the CBOR item is a text string or a byte string. In byte string literals the apostrophe has to be escaped.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing the same word in three different handwriting styles. They look different, but they all mean exactly the same thing.

sections.title: Two Enabling Grammar Changes
sections.content:
Empty data models. RFC 8610 required a CDDL file to have at least one rule. With CDDL modules, a file may use directives that bring in all of its rules, so the top-level rule becomes cddl = S *(rule S). The need for at least one rule becomes a semantic constraint checked after directives are processed.

Non-literal tag numbers and simple values. Tag numbers could only be written as literal unsigned integers. That made it impossible to express a range, such as the tag range 1668546817 to 1668612095 used by RFC 9277. The new head-number rule accepts either a uint or a type in angle brackets, so you can write #6.<ct-tag-number>(content) with ct-tag-number = 1668546817..1668612095. The same applies to simple values with #7.

Both changes are backward compatible, but CDDL that uses them may not be processed by existing implementations of RFC 8610.
sections.plainLanguage: First, a rule book is now allowed to be empty if it borrows its rules from elsewhere. Second, instead of naming one exact number, you can now say any number in this range.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The grammar changes are not believed to add security considerations beyond those in Section 5 of RFC 8610. The main concern is confusion in an environment that mixes CDDL tools, some updated and some not, particularly because of the string changes in Section 2 of the RFC.

An attacker could try to craft CDDL models that different parts of a system interpret differently, and the transition period offers one such opportunity. The RFC advises developers to treat CDDL models with the same care as any other source code, and notes that implementations using models operationally already need to check their provenance, authenticity and integrity. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If some tools read the new rules and some read the old ones, they might disagree, and a trickster could use that. So treat these files as carefully as program code.
